Current gas turbine engines are operating at pressure ratios around 25:1 and turbine inlet temperatures of 1600 K (2400°F).
Cycle study results indicate potential for further fuel savings by increasing pressure ratios up to 64:1 and turbine inlet temperatures over 1650 K (2500°F).
Combustor liner heat flux increases significantly with increasing inlet pressure, based on recent NASA experiments.
Experiments showed higher flame temperatures and radiant energy when using a fuel with 2% lower hydrogen content than Jet A, due to increased soot formation.
Existing radiation prediction models were unable to accurately capture the high radiant energy levels in the combustor secondary zone.

Transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layers on turbine blades is a major challenge, as the small disturbance theory used for external aerodynamics does not apply to the highly turbulent turbomachinery environment.
Film cooling is an increasingly important turbine blade cooling method, but optimization is challenging due to the complex interactions between coolant flow, main gas flow, and surface curvature.
Laser anemometer measurements have shown the Denton inviscid CFD code provides the best predictions of 3D velocity fields in turbine blade passages compared to other models.
Experiments on multi-pass turbine blade cooling passages have shown dramatic spikes in heat transfer coefficients at the 180-degree bends, very different from fully developed tube flow.
Verification of local coolant-side heat transfer coefficients at real engine conditions is extremely challenging due to the small size of the cooling passages.

NASA's HOST (Hot Section Technology) program is focused on producing improved design and analysis tools for predicting and designing gas turbine engine hot sections with improved reliability and durability.

Key research areas include fundamental experiments, analytical modeling of flow and heat transfer phenomena, and verification of advanced prediction techniques in facilities operating near real engine conditions.
Overcoming the current uncertainties in metal temperature prediction, which can be up to 100 K, is critical to enabling higher efficiency gas turbine engine cycles.
The iterative design process and need for 'overcooling' to ensure reliability adversely affects the ability to maximize cycle efficiency by minimizing cooling air usage.
Improved heat transfer design tools are needed to accurately predict combustor liner and turbine blade/vane temperatures and enable more reliable and durable hot section designs.
